title: TikTok and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Cross-Sectional Study of Social Media Content Quality
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the 100 most popular TikTok videos tagged #adhd. Two clinician raters, referencing the CADDRA and AAP ADHD practice guidelines, classified each video as useful, personal experience, or misleading, where misleading meant the video contained information lacking scientific evidence. 52% of the 100 videos were misleading: a quantitative share of items in a sample judged against an external clinical ground truth, i.e. a CONTENT estimate with a denominator.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language TikTok videos; authors based in Canada)
estimates.measure_type: % of the top 100 most-viewed TikTok videos tagged #adhd classified as misleading by clinician raters
estimates.denominator: 100 most-viewed TikTok videos tagged #adhd that met the inclusion criteria (out of the videos returned by the platform's popularity-ranked search on 18 July 2021)
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if it contained information lacking scientific evidence (e.g. unsubstantiated claims about treating ADHD), judged by clinician raters against the CADDRA and AAP ADHD practice guidelines; a personal-experience video that additionally contained generalized misleading statements was counted as misleading.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Videos were classified as misleading if it contained information lacking scientific evidence (e.g., unsubstantiated claims about treating ADHD)."
estimates.source_quote: Of the 100 videos meeting inclusion criteria, 52% (n = 52) were classified as misleading, 27% (n = 27) as personal experience, and 21% (n = 21) as useful.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results); Results, 'Videos Characteristics by Classification'; Table 3 column 'All (n = 100)'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: One psychiatrist and one psychiatry resident with clinical experience in ADHD independently classified every video, referencing the Canadian ADHD Resource Alliance (CADDRA) Canadian ADHD Practice Guidelines 4th ed. and the American Academy of Pediatrics ADHD Clinical Practice Guidelines; a third psychiatrist adjudicated disagreements. Inter-rater agreement 86%, kappa 0.7766 (P < 0.001).
estimates.moderator_quote: The TikTok mobile phone application was queried with a search for the hashtag "#adhd" on July 18, 2021 (Figure 1). The proprietary search algorithm returns the most popular videos based on the number of views and likes per video. [...] Videos were sorted in descending order by view count, and the inclusion criteria were applied until 100 videos were identified.
estimates.notes: Coded CONTENT rather than QUALITY: although the paper is framed as a study of 'content quality' and also applies PEMAT-A/V and JAMA instruments, the misleading/useful/personal-experience classification is an explicit veracity judgement against a stated external ground truth (national ADHD practice guidelines), and a wholly accurate video could not receive the 'misleading' label. Rank-truncated top-100 set within a single-hashtag corpus, hence denom_scope topical with denom_selection curated. No country is stated for the video sample; only non-English videos were excluded.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Creator-type subgroups were not extracted as separate rows: misleading videos were 55.1% (49/89) of non-HCP uploads and 27.3% (3/11) of HCP uploads (Table 3, Results). These are uploader subgroups of the same 100-video sample, and the 52% overall figure is the paper's headline; the subgroup split is available if an adjudicator wants source-type rows. (2) 'Useful' (21%) and 'personal experience' (27%) are the complementary categories of the same classification, not misinformation shares, so no rows. (3) Breakdown of error types inside the misleading videos (37/52 = 71% misattributed transdiagnostic symptoms; 8 = 15% misrepresented pathophysiology; 4 = 7% incorrect diagnostic approach; 2 = 4% misrepresented developmental theory; 1 = 2% non-validated coping strategies) is a typology within the misinformation-only subsample, not a falsity share, so not extracted. (4) PEMAT-A/V understandability (94.3%), actionability (14.3%) and JAMA (mean 1.3) are quality-instrument scores reported as means/percentages of scale points, not shares of items judged false; per the QUALITY rule and the 'means only' exclusion these give no prevalence row. (5) No exposure or sharing denominator is available: view and share counts are reported as per-video means, not as a share of a consumption denominator.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Sampling frame: TikTok in-app search for the hashtag #adhd on 18 July 2021, videos sorted descending by view count and inclusion criteria applied until 100 videos were reached (no random sampling; ads and deleted videos not retrievable). Coding: two clinician raters independently classified each video as useful, personal experience or misleading against CADDRA and AAP guidelines, with a third psychiatrist adjudicating disagreements; PEMAT-A/V and JAMA instruments also applied. Reliability as reported: 86% agreement, kappa 0.7766 (P < 0.001). No response-rate concept (content study).
rob.item6_quote: Videos were classified as misleading if it contained information lacking scientific evidence (e.g., unsubstantiated claims about treating ADHD). If a personal experience video additionally contained any generalized misleading statements, it was classified as misleading rather than personal experience.
rob.item10_quote: Of the 100 videos meeting inclusion criteria, 52% (n = 52) were classified as misleading, 27% (n = 27) as personal experience, and 21% (n = 21) as useful.
